# Estimative Language

> Copy of [Estimative Language](https://github.com/SOsintOps/intelligence-field-notes/blob/main/docs/estimative-language.md) from [Intelligence Field Notes](https://github.com/SOsintOps/intelligence-field-notes) 0.1.1. The original is the reference; this copy is here for offline use.

How to say how sure you are, so that the reader understands exactly what you meant. Two separate scales do two separate jobs: **likelihood** says how probable an event or development is; **confidence** says how good your basis is for saying so. Mixing them, or using words with no agreed meaning, is the most common way a sound analysis turns into a misleading report.

## Why Words Need Numbers
In 1951 a US National Intelligence Estimate said a Soviet attack on Yugoslavia was a "serious possibility". Sherman Kent, who led the Board of National Estimates, later asked the people who had agreed the text what odds they had meant: the answers ran from about 20 to 80 per cent. The same sentence, signed by everyone, had meant opposite things. Kent's essay *Words of Estimative Probability* (1964) proposed tying a few expressions to ranges of odds. The idea took decades to be adopted; ICD 203 is its descendant.

## The ICD 203 Likelihood Scale
ICD 203 gives two equivalent rows of terms. **Choose one row and use only that row** in a product: the directive strongly discourages mixing terms from different rows, and a product that does mix them must say explicitly that the terms express the same probability.

| Almost no chance | Very unlikely | Unlikely | Roughly even chance | Likely | Very likely | Almost certain(ly) |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| Remote | Highly improbable | Improbable (improbably) | Roughly even odds | Probable (probably) | Highly probable | Nearly certain |
| 01-05% | 05-20% | 20-45% | 45-55% | 55-80% | 80-95% | 95-99% |

These notes use the **first row**. A list such as "remote, very unlikely, unlikely, roughly even chance, likely, very likely, nearly certain" takes its ends from one row and its middle from the other: it is the mistake the directive warns against.

The scale stops at 99 and starts at 1. Certainty belongs to facts you observed, stated as facts; it is not a degree of likelihood.

## Confidence Levels
Confidence describes the analyst's basis for the judgement: the quantity and quality of the sources, the soundness of the logic, the understanding of the subject. A common three-level convention:

| Level | Meaning |
| :--- | :--- |
| **High confidence** | The judgement rests on high-quality information from several independent, reliable sources, and the reasoning is sound. It can still be wrong. |
| **Moderate confidence** | The information is credibly sourced and plausible, but not corroborated enough, or open to more than one interpretation. |
| **Low confidence** | The information is scant, questionable, fragmented or from a single doubtful source; the judgement is a lead to pursue, not a conclusion to act on. |

## The Rules
1.  **Never put a confidence level and a degree of likelihood in the same sentence.** ICD 203 forbids it to avoid confusion. "We assess with high confidence that it is very likely" states nothing a reader can use. Write two sentences, or choose the one that matters.
2.  **One row, all the way through.** Pick the likelihood row at the start and keep to it; templates should fix the row for you.
3.  **Likelihood is about events, confidence is about judgements.** "Very likely" qualifies something that may happen or may be the case; "high confidence" qualifies your assessment.
4.  **Explain the uncertainty, do not only label it.** Say what drives it: the age of the information, a single source, a gap, a key assumption. Say which indicator would change it.
5.  **Facts take no qualifier.** What you observed and captured is stated plainly, with its source. Qualifiers are for judgements.
6.  **No hedging words outside the scale.** "Could", "may", "might", "possibly", "it seems", "it is believed" carry no measurable meaning. Use "could" or "may" only with an explicit condition ("may move to another platform *if* the channel is banned"); otherwise use the scale.
7.  **Do not avoid the difficult judgement.** A report that qualifies everything as "roughly even chance" to be safe fails the accuracy standard as surely as one that overstates.

## Examples
| Instead of | Write |
| :--- | :--- |
| It is possible that the two accounts belong to the same person. | The two accounts are likely (55-80%) operated by the same person: they share a recovery e-mail and post in the same hours. |
| We assess with high confidence that the company is very likely a shell. | The company is very likely a shell company: no employees, no filed accounts, and a registered address shared with 412 other companies. We have high confidence in the registry data. |
| The group may be planning further attacks. | Further attacks by the group in the next three months are likely; the group has claimed one a month since March and announced a new campaign on 2 October. |
| Sources say the leader is in Dubai. | Two posts geolocated to Dubai Marina (S2, S4, both graded B2) place the leader in Dubai on 14 and 16 September. |

## Further Reading
- **"ICD 203: Analytic Standards"** (ODNI) - Section D.6.e.(2): the likelihood table and the rules quoted on this page. [PDF](https://www.dni.gov/files/documents/ICD/ICD-203.pdf)
- **"Words of Estimative Probability"** by Sherman Kent (*Studies in Intelligence*, vol. 8, no. 4, 1964) - The original argument for tying words to odds. [CIA page](https://www.cia.gov/resources/csi/studies-in-intelligence/archives/vol-8-no-4/words-of-estimative-probability/)
- **"Psychology of Intelligence Analysis"** by Richards J. Heuer Jr. - Chapter 12 on biases in estimating probabilities. [PDF](https://www.cia.gov/resources/csi/static/Pyschology-of-Intelligence-Analysis.pdf)
